papers.name: Paper 1: Computational thinking and programming skills
papers.covers: Fundamentals of algorithms, programming, and the theory behind them: tracing and writing code, subroutines, arrays, strings, validation, testing. Algorithms in the question paper are written in AQA pseudo-code, which AQA publishes as a Notes and guidance document. Program code figures, and every coded answer you write, are in the one language your paper is set in: you sit 8525A/1, 8525B/1 or 8525C/1 for C#, Python or VB.NET. You do not have to write your own pseudo-code in AQA's style; it only has to be clear and unambiguous. Written paper. Worth 50% of the GCSE. No calculator. Some questions ask you to write a complete program or subroutine on paper.

papers.name: Paper 2: Computing concepts
papers.covers: Data representation, computer systems, networks, cyber security, relational databases and SQL, ethical, legal and environmental impacts. Written paper. Worth 50% of the GCSE. No calculator, so binary and hexadecimal conversions are done by hand. Includes a mix of short answers, calculations and extended responses.

commandWords.meaning: One-mark recall. A word, a number or a short phrase; no explanation wanted.
Say what something is or how it works, in order. No reasons needed.
Give reasons. Every point needs a "because" or a "so", and the number of marks tells you how many linked points.
Write code, an algorithm or pseudo-code. Use your paper's language or clear pseudo-code; the marks are for correct logic, so a small syntax slip is not fatal, but structure is.
Fill in the gaps in a trace table, a truth table, a program or a diagram. Work through it line by line.
Multiple choice. Shade exactly one answer; if you change your mind, cross it out clearly and shade another.
Take forward or build upon given information. You are handed working code or a part-answer and must add to it, not start from scratch.
Show the working. Binary, hexadecimal and file-size calculations need each step written down, with units.
Give similarities and differences, mentioning both things in each point.
Longer answers, usually about impacts or trade-offs. Give points on more than one side, link them, and finish with a judgement.
Give the precise meaning of a technical term, using the specification's wording where you can.
Support your choice with evidence. Say what you picked and why it is the right pick for this problem, not just what it is.
Present a possible case or solution. There is no single right answer, so give one that fits the scenario and say how it fits.
Further develop code or an answer you have been given. Keep what is there and add to it.
Produce a diagram, such as a logic circuit or a flowchart. Use pencil and label it.

assessmentObjectives.meaning: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the key concepts and principles of computer science. Nearly all of the AO1 marks are on Paper 2 (25.6% of the total, against 4.4% on Paper 1), so Paper 2 rewards precise recall.
Apply knowledge and understanding of key concepts and principles of computer science: trace and complete code, convert and calculate.

Analyse problems in computational terms, to make reasoned judgements and to design, program, evaluate and refine solutions. Nearly all of the AO3 marks are on Paper 1 (25.6% against 4.4%), so Paper 1 is where designing, writing and refining code earns its marks.

grade9ByQuestionType.questionType: Trace a program or subroutine (AO2, 3 to 6 marks)
grade9ByQuestionType.looksLike: A trace table with one column per variable, values written only when they change, output recorded on the right, and the final state read off correctly, including what a function returns.

grade9ByQuestionType.questionType: Write a program or subroutine (AO3, 6 to 12 marks)
grade9ByQuestionType.looksLike: Correct structure first: subroutine header with parameters, sensible variable names, the right loop for the job, input validated, output at the end. Every requirement in the question is met and the code is indented so the examiner can follow it.

grade9ByQuestionType.questionType: Explain a programming concept (AO1, 2 to 4 marks)
grade9ByQuestionType.looksLike: Uses the specification term, gives a reason and a concrete example: "a local variable exists only inside the subroutine, so two subroutines can both use a variable called total without interfering".
Test data chosen for normal, boundary and erroneous cases with the expected result for each, and validation rules that match the data being checked.

grade9ByQuestionType.questionType: Extended response (AO1 to AO3, 6 to 9 marks)
grade9ByQuestionType.looksLike: A structured answer that names the concepts, applies them to the scenario in the question, and reaches a conclusion. Level-marked, so vocabulary and organisation both count.
